explanations.explanation: I get why you'd picture something grand, friend, since David constructs buildings for himself in the same verse. But the text says he prepared a place for the ark and “…pitched a tent for it.” A tent, not a stone temple. Same ark, humbler roof.

That's right, friend. David builds for himself, but for the ark he “…pitched a tent for it.” No stone temple shows up in this passage at all. I spent years in a kitchen junk drawer, so believe me, I respect a humble roof.
Yes, friend. David says, “No one but the Levites may carry the ark of God…” He says it plain, with no wiggle room. When the rule is that clear, the best move is to follow it.

The elders do show up later, going along with David with rejoicing (1 Chronicles 15:25). But carrying the ark isn't their job. David's rule names one group only: the Levites. Going along with the ark and carrying it are two different jobs.
Strong guys make sense for heavy lifting, friend. But this passage doesn't hand the ark to any soldiers. David says no one but the Levites may carry it. Muscle isn't the qualification here.

That's the word, friend. David says the LORD has “…chosen them to carry the ark of the LORD and to minister before Him forever.” The Levites didn't win this job by trying out for it. It was given to them by the LORD's choice.

Training sounds sensible, friend, because carrying something that precious sounds like a skill. But David doesn't say the Levites were trained for it. He says the LORD has “chosen” them. Their job starts with the LORD's choice.

No résumé, no interview, no hiring committee here. David says the LORD has “…chosen them to carry the ark of the LORD…” I was bought for a quarter at a closing bakery, and even I know that's not the same as being chosen for something big. This job came from the LORD's choice.

That's it, friend. David tells them, “You and your relatives must consecrate yourselves so that you may bring the ark of the LORD, the God of Israel, to the place I have prepared for it.” That means they set themselves apart before the job begins. They get ready first, and the carrying comes second.

Counting is a fair guess, since the list of clans comes with a lot of numbers. But the command David gives in this verse isn't a headcount. He says they and their relatives must consecrate themselves. Counting is just the tally, and consecrating is the instruction.

Armor would look impressive, friend, but nobody is going to battle here. David tells them to consecrate themselves so they can bring the ark to the place he prepared. The preparation is about them being set apart. Nothing in the verse mentions armor.

Yes, friend. David says, “It was because you Levites were not with us the first time that the LORD our God burst forth in anger against us.” He gives that reason right to the Levite heads. This time David makes sure they are there.

explanations.answer: They moved the ark at night
explanations.explanation: The text never mentions a nighttime move, friend. The reason David gives is that the Levites “…were not with us the first time…” I wouldn't add a reason David didn't give. We stick to the one he said.

David says “us,” which means he was part of that first try. So the problem wasn't David being missing. He tells the Levite heads, “It was because you Levites were not with us the first time…” The missing group was the Levites.

That's right, friend. David says, “For we did not consult Him about the proper order.” He owns it with the word “we,” and that includes himself. A king saying we missed it is a good example for the rest of us.
I can see why this one is tricky, but it's actually True. David says, “For we did not consult Him about the proper order.” He puts himself in that “we.” He doesn't hide it.

Yes, friend. The text says, “…the Levites carried the ark of God on their shoulders with the poles…” It also says this was what Moses had commanded. The first try used a new cart (1 Chronicles 13:7), and this time the ark goes by shoulders and poles.

explanations.answer: On a cart pulled by oxen
explanations.explanation: That's how the first try went, friend. They put the ark on a new cart (1 Chronicles 13:7), and the oxen stumbled (1 Chronicles 13:9). This time the Levites carry it “…on their shoulders with the poles…” So this round has no cart at all.

explanations.answer: On a chariot pulled by horses
explanations.explanation: A chariot would make for a fast entrance, friend. But the text says the Levites carried the ark “…on their shoulders with the poles…” No horses are mentioned anywhere. Shoulders and poles, as Moses had commanded.

That's right, friend. The Levites carry the ark “…as Moses had commanded in accordance with the word of the LORD.” Moses was Israel's leader long before David's day (Exodus 3:10). Carrying it this way wasn't a new idea. It was an old command being followed.

Samuel was a prophet in Israel (1 Samuel 3:20), so I see why his name comes to mind. But this verse names someone else as the one who gave the command. It says the Levites carried the ark “…as Moses had commanded in accordance with the word of the LORD.” Moses is the name in the text.

Joshua led Israel after Moses (Joshua 1:1 to 2), so he's a fair guess. But the verse doesn't name him here. It says “…as Moses had commanded in accordance with the word of the LORD.” Moses is the one who gets the credit in this verse.

Yes, friend. David tells the leaders to appoint their relatives “…as singers to lift up their voices with joy…” The harps, lyres and cymbals go along with the singing. This parade is going to have a soundtrack.

Writing it all down would be a handy job, friend. But the verse doesn't send the relatives out with pens. It says they're appointed “as singers.” The instruments are for making music, not taking notes.

Runners would get the word out fast, friend. But the verse says these relatives are appointed “…as singers to lift up their voices…” That's the job the text gives them. The harps, lyres and cymbals go along with the singing.
That's the word, friend. David wants the singers “…to lift up their voices with joy…” The harps, lyres and cymbals go with it. The whole assignment is a happy one.

Sorrow doesn't fit this plan, friend. The verse says the singers are to lift up their voices “with joy.” That's a day for celebrating. The sad songs can stay in the back of the junk drawer I got called out of years ago.

I get why fear comes to mind, since the first try with the ark ended in the LORD's anger (1 Chronicles 15:13). But the verse says the singers are to lift up their voices “with joy.” That's the word David uses. This round has a joyful sound.

It's the other way around this time, friend. The text says that “…God helped the Levites who were carrying the ark of the covenant of the LORD…” The anger belongs to the first try that David talked about. This time the Levites are carrying the ark the way the text says, and God helps them.

That's right, friend. The text says that “…God helped the Levites who were carrying the ark of the covenant of the LORD…” There's no anger this time, only help. And in that same verse, they sacrificed seven bulls and seven rams.

explanations.answer: Sacrifice seven bulls and seven rams
explanations.explanation: Yes, friend. The text says, “…because God helped the Levites who were carrying the ark of the covenant of the LORD, they sacrificed seven bulls and seven rams.” God's help comes first, and then the sacrifice follows. That's seven and seven, so there's a lot of sacrificing going on.

explanations.answer: Rest seven days beside the road
explanations.explanation: The seven is right, friend, but the action is different. The text says they “…sacrificed seven bulls and seven rams.” because God helped them. There's no seven-day rest in this passage. Seven bulls and seven rams is what the verse gives us.

explanations.answer: Set up stones to mark the spot
explanations.explanation: Marking the spot is a nice idea, but it isn't in this verse. The text says that because God helped the Levites, “…they sacrificed seven bulls and seven rams.” That's what they do after God's help. No stones are stacked in this passage.

Yes, friend. The text says David “…was dressed in a robe of fine linen, as were all the Levites who were carrying the ark…” The singers and Chenaniah, the director of music, wear it too. Everybody looks like they belong on the same team.

I can see why you'd think the king would stand out, but it's actually True. The text says David “…was dressed in a robe of fine linen, as were all the Levites who were carrying the ark…” The Levites match him. The text also says David wore a linen ephod.

That's right, friend. The text says all Israel brought up the ark “…with shouting, with the sounding of rams’ horns and trumpets, and with cymbals and the music of harps and lyres.” Nobody is whispering here. That's a loud parade.

Silence would be a very quiet parade, friend, and this one isn't. The text says they brought up the ark “…with shouting, with the sounding of rams’ horns and trumpets…” Add the cymbals, harps and lyres, and silence doesn't have a chance.

Fasting is a fair guess for a serious day, but it isn't in this verse. The text says all Israel brought up the ark “…with shouting, with the sounding of rams’ horns and trumpets…” The verse is about noise, and a lot of it.

Yes, friend. Michal, Saul's daughter, “…looked down from a window and saw King David dancing and celebrating…” The king isn't standing off to the side. He's right in the celebration. And the verse says she “…despised him in her heart.”

explanations.answer: King David weeping beside the ark
explanations.explanation: This is a day of rejoicing, friend, but the text doesn't mention weeping at all. It says Michal “…saw King David dancing and celebrating…” That's what she sees from the window. Dancing and celebrating is the answer the verse gives.

explanations.answer: King David arguing with the priests
explanations.explanation: The priests are busy in this passage, but the text never shows them arguing. Zadok and Abiathar are named earlier, and priests blow the trumpets before the ark (1 Chronicles 15:24). What Michal sees from the window is “…King David dancing and celebrating…” The only sour thing in the verse is what she feels in her heart.
